Google's biggest ranking "buckets", according to evidence collected at its antitrust trial, are:

1. Topicality: How relevant is the page to a topic/query. Heavily determined by the "ABC" ranking signals:
• Anchors - the links pointing to the page
• Body - the text on the page
• Clicks - user click signals to determine relevance

2. Navboost: a re-ranking system that uses 13 months of user click data to adjust search results (first/long/last clicks)

3. Quality (Q*): One of Google's most important signals, based on site authority + quality adjustments (e.g., Panda, Helpful Content, spam)

SEOs—including yours truly—often get distracted by shiny things. But focusing on these three ranking buckets will likely account for 80-90% of your Google visibility.

I'm pretty confident these are ChatGPT fan-out queries in Google Search Console.

You can use this regex filter to check your own sites:

(?i)(site:.*official|official.*site:)

It checks for site: and "official" at the same time. It's not *all* ChatGPT queries, but it's the ones that contain both of those terms.

I just used this across a few sites and I'm seeing the same pattern of many impressions, 0 clicks, and a whole lot of queries that look exactly like ChatGPT fan-outs in GSC.

What does ChatGPT search for when someone asks about your brand? 👀

@mjcachon  analyzed 189 branded prompts across 723 GPT-5.5 runs, identifying 1,797 fan-out subqueries:

* 10.3 distinct subqueries per prompt across 4 runs
* 93.4% included the brand
* 30.2% used site:
* 23.8% used exact-match quotes
* 10.1% investigated reputation and trust
* Only 0.8% mentioned competitors

The typical sequence: ask broadly > narrow to a domain > verify exact claims > reformulate if needed.

A great reminder that indexability, clear corporate information, consistency, freshness, official profiles, reputation and migration hygiene all influence branded AI visibility.

Google drops (some) Site Reputation Abuse policy penalties in Europe, but publishers shouldn't celebrate

Here's what you need to know:

"Site Reputation Abuse" is, broadly, when a strong site publishes (monetized) third-party content that probably wouldn't rank on its own, but rides the coattails of the strong site in order to make money.

For example, Forbes publishing low-value coupon pages from a third-party supplier.

Google typically applies a manual penalty to those pages, causing them to disappear from search results. But now, EU regulations mean that the manual penalty will *no longer apply in the EU*, and those pages can technically rank again.

BUT... Google is also creating a workaround to seemingly circumvent EU regulations. Instead of dropping those pages from search results, Google will *separate* the penalized sections from the main site, so they will be forced to rank on their own, which they likely won't do.

In the end, those penalized site sections will likely STILL have no visibility.

This is another example of Google technically complying with the law while still achieving its desired result. And they are very, very good at this. 

So don't revive those parasite SEO strategies just yet.

🚨 The #SEOFOMO State of AI Search Optimization Report – 2026 Edition is here 👇

The results are in! 171 search professionals from 36 countries answered this year’s SEOFOMO State of AI Search Optimization survey between 17 and 27 August, and there’s a lot in here… including how much has shifted since last year’s edition.

Some key insights:

* 98% of respondents have had a client, manager or decision maker ask about AI search visibility, up from 91% last year. The bigger jump is budget: 69% now have it allocated, versus 38% in 2025. 61% say their investment grew during 2026, and only 1% saw it cut.

* 75% have a dedicated AI search optimization strategy for at least some of their sites, up from 51%. 92% are tracking AI visibility and citations, up from 78%. And the share saying nobody owns this work dropped from 11% to 4%, someone’s finally in charge.

* The SEO team leads it for 77% of respondents, basically where it was last year at 75%, and most budget still lives inside SEO. Standalone AI search budgets grew from around 5% to 15%, so they exist now, they’re just not the norm.

* ChatGPT leads, followed by Google’s AI search surfaces and Gemini. This is multi-platform work already.

* 56% report at least some positive business impact, though only 5% call it significant, 28% see none yet, and 5% report a negative impact. The share attributing more than 5% of site revenue to AI search more than doubled, from 8% to 19%. But 46% still put it at 0-5%, and 35% can’t tell what it contributes at all.

I'm coming back to X after quite a long break 🔥. You can expect from me tips on SEO and improving AI search visibility. 

I will start with sharing my setup for analyzing GSC, @screamingfrog  data and AI search visibility data via MCP.

Now I connect each tool over MCP and ask my questions in plain language. The model picks the right query, runs it, and reads the result back to me.

Here's my setup:
1️⃣ Search Console data → I pipe it into and connect to the official Google BigQuery MCP. Then I ask things like "which pages rank well but barely get clicks?" or "was this week's drop a clicks problem or an impressions problem?"
2️⃣ AI visibility → Peec AI MCP. Which engines am I winning, who's beating me in the prompts I track, and which sources do the models actually cite.
3️⃣ Technical SEO → Screaming Frog MCP (native since v24.0). I ask for a crawl in plain English and follow up with "what changed since last crawl?" instead of diffing two exports.

And when a tool has no MCP yet? I point Claude Code at the API docs, or just hand it the CSV. Either way I'm back to asking the right questions instead of building pivots.
